title: Opt-Out Time Machine for AI Training Compliance
one_liner: A historical archive of every site's machine-readable AI-training opt-outs (robots.txt, TDMRep, ai.txt, meta tags, headers) so model builders can prove what was reserved on the day they crawled.
customer: AI startups and labs that train or fine-tune on scraped or third-party data (especially EU-exposed), dataset publishers, and rights-holder groups (publishers, collecting societies) that need proof of their own reservations.
problem: GPAI obligations have applied since Aug 2025 and AI Office enforcement began in Aug 2026. Providers need a copyright policy and must respect machine-readable rights reservations under the EU text-and-data-mining exception (background, verify). Opt-out signals change over time and nobody retains neutral evidence of what a site said on a given day, yet disputes will turn on exactly that.
solution: A weekly crawl of the top ~50M domains capturing robots.txt, /.well-known/tdmrep.json, ai.txt, meta tags, headers and terms-page hashes, stored as signed, timestamped snapshots. API calls answer 'what did domain X reserve at time T?' and 'filter dataset D by reservations as of T'. Certificates of compliance for training corpora and monitoring alerts for rights holders whose reservations are ignored.
why_now: Enforcement powers over GPAI providers began Aug 2026, copyright-and-training cases are moving through European courts, and crawl and storage costs are low enough for a two-person team.
revenue_model: API subscriptions of $2-25k/month for labs and dataset teams, $5-30k per compliance certificate, and $500-5k/month for rights-holder monitoring.
non_obvious_insight: Compliance evidence is a time-series problem. The neutral party that started archiving earlier owns the truth, and it cannot be recreated retroactively, so the moat begins accumulating on day one.
first_30_days: Crawl the top 1M domains weekly (a few hundred dollars a month) and publish a free opt-out prevalence report. Sign three EU AI startups or dataset publishers to paid pilots of $2-5k and approach one collecting society.

title: Fish Settlement Audit Becoming the Fleet's Payment Rail
one_liner: Start by auditing settlement sheets against fish tickets to recover missed money, then become the split-pay rail that routes each settlement to crew, lessors, lenders and the IRS.
customer: Skippers and permit holders who pay $99 flat or 15% of any recovered amount for the audit. Crew use the shares calculator free. Later, skippers and quota lessors pay about 0.3-0.5% of settlement flow for split-pay, and lenders and CFEC-adjacent programs pay referral fees.
problem: The 'price' you're paid is a stack: base price, quality bonuses (for example $0.15 RSW, $0.05 bleeding, $0.05 chilling), loyalty or volume bonuses, post-season retros, and deductions for ice, fuel, gear advances and storage. Every processor's sheet looks different. The fisherman's own copy of the fish ticket sits in a Ziploc in the wheelhouse and never gets matched against the settlement. Nobody checks. Then the whole lump lands in one skipper's account weeks later and he has to act as the bank for crew shares, quota lease payments, loan payments, gear vendors and self-employment tax. That is where disputes, missed quarterly taxes and stiffed crew come from.
solution: Audit: photograph the settlement sheet and fish tickets, and an LLM parses pounds, price stack, bonuses and deductions, flags weight mismatches, missed quality bonuses, wrong grades and unexplained deductions, and prints a plain-English 'you were owed' letter. A crew shares calculator generates crew settlement sheets from the skipper's expense rules. Rail: once trust exists, route the settlement into a virtual account that auto-splits per signed crew share agreement, quota lease, loan payments, vendor invoices and a tax set-aside, with instant partial payments.
why_now: Final settlements for the 2026 salmon season are landing right now (Oct-Dec). Price swung from $1.03 to $1.72 in one year, so fishermen are checking. Vision LLMs can read messy sheets at near-zero cost. Banking-as-a-service and real-time payment rails make split-pay possible for a small team. Crew who waited about four years for crab disaster relief also learned that clean earnings paperwork is worth money.
revenue_model: Audit: $99 flat or 15% of recovery. Rail: 0.3-0.5% of settlement flow plus interchange and float. Later: earned-wage advances against booked settlements, lender referrals, claim-packet prep for federal disaster relief (crew earnings vaults double as the proof), and an anonymized price tape sold to buyers and lenders.
non_obvious_insight: The skipper is the fleet's unlicensed bank, and nobody has both documents in one place. The audit is the trojan horse: it gets a fisherman to hand over settlement history, which is exactly the underwriting and routing data needed for the rail. The settlement sheet is a stack of price components, and the money is hidden in the parts nobody reads.
first_30_days: Post in fishermen's Facebook groups: 'free settlement check, send the sheet.' Process 100 sheets by hand plus LLM, log every error found, and turn 5-10 recoveries into case studies. Build the crew share calculator as a free viral wedge. Charge 15% of recovered amounts above $500. Start collecting the anonymized price stack by port, species and processor.

title: Caring Contacts as a Service for Hospitals
one_liner: Outsourced, human-edited follow-up messages and calls after a suicide-risk emergency visit or crisis call, run on a compliance-grade platform hospitals and 988 centers can buy per patient.
customer: Hospital EDs and behavioral units, state-funded 988 crisis centers, university counseling centers and behavioral-health carve-out plans, paying $40-120 per patient enrolled or $5-15k a month per site.
problem: The highest-risk window is the weeks after discharge or a crisis call. The Joint Commission's NPSG 15.01.01 requires follow-up policy, and randomized trials of brief, non-demanding 'caring contact' messages show fewer attempts. Yet most systems run this through one overwhelmed staffer mailing postcards, with no delivery guarantee, tracking or outcome reporting.
solution: A managed service: enrollment at discharge on a tablet, a cadence built from an evidence-based message library (days 1, 3, 7, 14, 30 and beyond), AI drafting with human review, two-way replies routed to trained staff, escalation with warm handoff to crisis lines, and EHR-connected dashboards for Joint Commission and Zero Suicide reporting.
why_now: 988 volume has grown since 2022, about a dozen states now levy 988 telecom fees that fund local centers, and the Harvard study estimating 4,400 fewer youth and young-adult suicide deaths in 988's first 2.5 years strengthens the funding case. 988 politics (Press 3 ended Jul 2025, a restored version excluding Trevor Project announced Jun 2026) push centers toward reliable, defensible operations.
revenue_model: Per-enrollee fee plus platform fee, funded by hospital quality budgets, state 988 funds and SAMHSA grants.
non_obvious_insight: The market chases AI that detects risk, but the best-evidenced and cheapest intervention is a human-sent, non-demanding note. The product is operations and proof (reliable delivery, documentation, outcome reporting), not detection.
first_30_days: Partner with one county crisis center and one hospital ED. Write the message library with a clinical advisor who knows the caring-contacts literature. Enroll 100 patients on a $10k pilot and measure re-contact and re-presentation rates.

title: Cryo-Vault for Artisan Food Microbial Cultures
one_liner: Backup-and-rescue service that fingerprints, isolates and cryo-banks the living house cultures (cheese rind flora, koji, kombucha SCOBYs, sourdough starters, mushroom spawn, natural-wine yeast) of small food producers in split-geography -80 storage, with a 48-hour emergency revival.
customer: Small artisan producers: raw-milk and farmstead cheesemakers, koji, miso and sake makers, kombucha brewers, specialty mushroom growers, sourdough bakeries, natural winemakers and cideries. Pay $250-400 intake plus $20-40/month per culture, and $400-600 per emergency rescue.
problem: A small producer's house culture is their product identity, yet it lives on the counter or in a single fridge, propagated by serial subculture. Mother cultures senesce and drift, contaminate, or get wiped out by phage (dairy) or Trichoderma-type molds (mushrooms). One crash can end a brand for months. Big culture houses won't bank a small producer's strains, and commercial biobank services are priced and designed for pharma.
solution: A mail-in kit: send a gram of culture, get back an ITS/16S-based composition fingerprint, viability and purity report, and isolated key strains. Each is banked as glycerol stocks in triplicate at two separate sites, with a dashboard of banked cultures. The rescue tier revives a viable working culture in 48 hours with contamination diagnosis, and later adds a periodic 'drift check' compared against the banked baseline. Optional fingerprint certificates for craft-authenticity claims and geographic-indication programs.
why_now: Fermentation and koji-based craft food is booming, and sequencing costs are trivial (about $30 per amplicon sample). Consolidation and climate stress are raising the cost of a culture crash. Small food makers increasingly market on 'living' and heritage claims that they can't currently back up. Laid-off microbiologists can staff this cheaply.
revenue_model: Intake fee plus recurring monthly vault subscription per culture. Per-event rescue fees. Fingerprint certificates and drift-check add-ons. Later B2B with food-safety consultants and craft trade associations, which bundle it as a member benefit.
non_obvious_insight: Cryo-banking with a genetic fingerprint is routine bench hygiene for any wet-lab, but the food world has never been offered it at a price small producers can pay. Nobody thinks of 'my sourdough' as a strain to back up until it crashes. The wedge is not the science, it is the packaging as insurance and the rescue promise.
first_30_days: Bank 10 cultures for free from friendly producers (cheesemakers, kombucha and mushroom growers) recruited through guild forums and Facebook groups. Rent -80 space at a university core, a co-lab or a local biobank. Use a commercial amplicon sequencing service for fingerprints. Publish one story about a rescued culture. Convert the first cohort to $99/month founding-member pricing. Stay strictly with BSL-1 food-grade organisms and set clear policies on pathogen refusal and shipping.

title: Through-the-Package Drug Verification Library
one_liner: A subscription spectral fingerprint library and scan-on-receipt workflow that lets pharmacies and wholesalers verify what is actually in a sealed vial or blister pack, using off-the-shelf handheld Raman/NIR devices.
customer: 503A/503B compounding pharmacies and telehealth GLP-1 dispensers receiving vials or API from overseas, secondary wholesalers and repackagers, hospital pharmacies, and med-spa distributors.
problem: ARPA-H states that drug-related morbidity and mortality cost $528 billion per year, that recalls affect the medication of over 150 million Americans each year, that 'most recalls only happen after patients are exposed', and that only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports, a process that takes weeks. Serialization under DSCSA tracks the box (package-level identifiers, 24-hour notification of illegitimate product), not the molecule inside it, so a convincing counterfeit or diluted vial passes every paperwork check.
solution: Do not build hardware. Rent or resell existing handheld Raman/NIR units, and build the proprietary part: a reference library of authentic and adulterated finished-dose spectra measured through blisters, vials and prefilled pens, plus a classifier and a chain-of-custody report (photo, lot number, spectrum, pass/fail/uncertain). Uncertain results route to a partner lab for confirmatory HPLC. The library improves with every scan.
why_now: ARPA-H's FASTPASS program (solicitation ARPA-H-SOL-26-160; solution summaries due September 21, 2026, full proposals November 10, 2026) is funding through-packaging sensing (TA1 SAMPLE) and analytics (TA2 DETECT), which signals that the sensing hardware and spectroscopy science are mature enough to commercialize. GLP-1 volume and compounding have widened the exposure of small dispensers who have no way to check incoming product.
revenue_model: $1 to $3 per scan (usage SaaS), $300 per month device rental, $150 to $400 per escalated lab confirmation, and $6k to $24k per year library license for wholesalers.
non_obvious_insight: DSCSA verifies labels and traceability, not contents, and ARPA-H itself says the gap is one 'no single agency, manufacturer, or current technology can close alone'. That leaves room for a private data product. The moat is the library of through-package spectra, not the scanner, and it compounds with every customer scan. Evidence: https://arpa-h.gov/explore-funding/programs/fastpass ($528B, 150M Americans, 'only a small percentage of imported drugs are sampled and tested at ports', TA1 SAMPLE and TA2 DETECT) and https://www.fda.gov/drugs/drug-supply-chain-integrity/drug-supply-chain-security-act-dscsa (package-level identification and 24-hour illegitimate-product notification). Caveat: the ARPA-H page did not give product types or counterfeit prevalence, and the GLP-1 exposure is my inference from public FDA alerts.
first_30_days: Pick 10 high-volume SKUs (injectable GLP-1 vials and pens plus a few high-value generics). Buy authentic references, make in-house dilution and wrong-API samples with a partner lab, rent two handhelds, and collect spectra through the packaging. Offer 3 compounding pharmacies and 2 regional wholesalers a free 30-day pilot with scan-on-receipt. Convert to paid on a per-scan plan. Skip the FASTPASS proposal unless a university partner handles it.

title: Verified-MW Truth Feed for Data Center Load
one_liner: A probability score and satellite-plus-permit verification of every large-load request, so planners and investors can tell the real 42 GW from the 201 GW of paper.
customer: Utility load-forecast and IRP teams, ISOs, state PUC staff and consumer advocates. Hedge funds, infrastructure investors and equipment makers buy the same feed as alternative data.
problem: About 36.6 GW is under construction versus about 201 GW 'in planning'. Developers file duplicate requests at several utilities, utilities over-forecast, and ratepayers fund the generation and wires built for load that never shows up. Even xAI's Memphis battery is '2.8 GWh counted versus 3.3 GWh claimed' and nobody verifies it.
solution: Fuse interconnection filings, zoning and permit records, tax abatements, transformer and switchgear procurement signals, construction imagery (SAR and optical), thermal signatures of cooling plants and tariff deposits into a per-project probability of energization by date and MW online. Ship it as an API, quarterly reports and exhibits usable in regulatory proceedings.
why_now: Large-load requests are exploding, utilities are adding deposit rules, and cheap satellite data plus LLM document parsing lets a three-person team do this.
revenue_model: $30-500k a year per investor subscription and $75-300k per utility or ISO, with discounted licenses for consumer advocates.
non_obvious_insight: The most expensive number in the grid is the load forecast, and it is built from self-reported requests. Hedge funds already want the same data for AI-capex tracking, so they can fund a public-interest product.
first_30_days: Build datasets for Virginia, Ohio and Texas. Publish a 'phantom load index'. Sell three alternative-data subscriptions at $30-50k. Offer free trials to two consumer advocate offices.

title: Robot Access Passport for Commercial Buildings
one_liner: One certified robot identity, insurance certificate and elevator/door gateway that lets any delivery, cleaning or humanoid robot enter a building, with landlords collecting a fee.
customer: Owners and managers of office towers, multifamily REITs, hospitals, hotels and malls, who pay a subscription. Robot operators pay per-robot access fees.
problem: Every robot vendor negotiates separately with building management on elevator integration, insurance, liability and hours. Buildings have no policy or tooling, and incidents have no clear owner. This gets worse as sidewalk, cleaning, security and humanoid pilots multiply.
solution: A $1-2k building-side controller integrated with elevators, doors and turnstiles through existing vendor APIs or relays, plus a registry that verifies operator, insurance, firmware version and incident hotline. A policy engine sets quiet hours, zones and speed limits, with usage-based billing. Landlords earn a share of access fees, and robot operators integrate once for many buildings.
why_now: About 22k humanoids shipped in H1 2026, delivery robots and drones are moving to multifamily, and regulators (NHTSA's July 2026 first-responder letter) are pushing for accountability. Buildings are the next permission bottleneck.
revenue_model: $150-400 a month per building in SaaS plus $5-15 per robot per month in access fees, split with the landlord, and installation margin.
non_obvious_insight: The scarce resource in robot deployment is permission, and building owners are the gatekeepers with zero tooling. A neutral gatekeeper standard is a two-sided network, like 'ID.me plus a certificate of insurance for robots', and landlords get paid to adopt it.
first_30_days: Approach 2 property managers in one metro where delivery robots already operate. Build an integration for one elevator vendor's open API, get a certificate-of-insurance template from a broker, and charge $500 a month for the pilot.

title: Vet Tech Apprenticeship Intermediary
one_liner: Registered-apprenticeship sponsorship as a service, letting clinics grow their own technicians through a paid pathway with wage support and retention contracts.
customer: Clinics and groups with 3 or more open assistant or tech roles, plus state workforce boards that fund apprenticeships.
problem: Figures from a trade opinion piece (directional only): about 2 techs per vet versus a 4:1 ideal, most techs leave within 4 years, techs average about $45K, program enrollment is down 43%, and only about 7,000 of 14,000 needed new techs sit for licensing exams each year. Clinics cannot release staff for classroom time, and on-the-job training is unstructured.
solution: We register and manage an apprenticeship program as sponsor of record. Each apprentice pairs with an accredited distance-learning tech program, an on-site mentor (trained by us), a competency logbook and a wage-step schedule with a retention agreement. We file paperwork for state and workforce-board funds and track progress toward the licensing exam.
why_now: There is a 2025-26 push at the federal and state level to expand apprenticeships and fund workforce pathways (verify state programs). A new supervised professional tier (Colorado's VPA) raises demand for skilled support staff, and clinics are desperate for retention tools.
revenue_model: $250-400 per apprentice per month, a $500 clinic setup fee, and a share of state grants. Multi-clinic groups pay for program licenses.
non_obvious_insight: The shortage is discussed as 'not enough schools'. The real bottleneck is that employers cannot afford to release staff and have no retention hook. An apprenticeship converts an assistant already on payroll into a tech, with public money and a contract that keeps them.
first_30_days: Map which states permit apprenticeship or on-the-job routes to licensing and pick two. Get 3-5 clinics to commit 1-2 apprentices each. Partner with an accredited distance program. Begin state registration and charge a $500 setup fee to lock in clinics.

title: Court-Ready Satellite Emission Evidence for Litigators
one_liner: Expert-witness-grade reports that use hourly geostationary pollution data to document emission events at large industrial sources.
customer: Environmental plaintiffs' firms, community groups with litigation funders, state attorney general offices, and insurers or investors assessing pollution liability.
problem: As federal enforcement priorities shifted in 2025-26 (prior knowledge), private litigation and state action fill the gap. Those actors need independent, admissible evidence, and most cannot interpret satellite data.
solution: Case-specific 'Emission Event Reports' for large point sources (power plants, refineries, LNG terminals, petrochemical complexes). They combine hourly NO2, SO2 and HCHO enhancements from geostationary sounders (NASA TEMPO in North America, Sentinel-4 in Europe), wind reanalysis and thermal flare data, with documented chain of custody and academic expert witnesses.
why_now: Hourly pollution monitoring from geostationary orbit is new: TEMPO has been operating since 2023-24 and Sentinel-4 launched in 2025. Regulatory retreat drives demand for private evidence.
revenue_model: $15-60k per case report. Retainer for firms with recurring dockets. Expert-testimony fees.
non_obvious_insight: Litigation budgets grow when regulation shrinks. A method that survives a Daubert challenge is a defensible moat, because courts reward the first tested method.
first_30_days: Partner with an atmospheric scientist willing to serve as expert. Build a report template on three well-known refinery or power-plant events. Present to five environmental plaintiffs' firms and one state AG office, and sign a first paid case.

title: Stablecoin Depeg and Freeze Cover
one_liner: GENIUS made stablecoins legal, not insured. Sell corporate treasurers parametric cover for issuer depeg, redemption suspension and wallet freezes so their risk committees will approve holding balances.
customer: Treasurers and CFOs at mid-market and payments companies holding $1M-$100M in USDC or USDT, including corporate clients of the new Citi and Coinbase flow.
problem: GENIUS gives holders priority claims but no deposit insurance. USDT is about $140B and USDC about $74B, the Senate Democrats' Tether report alleges $2B of Iranian flows against $550M frozen, and Bitcoin has drawn down about 50%. Auditors and risk committees want risk transfer, and there is none.
solution: Parametric cover that pays when a named stablecoin trades below a threshold (for example $0.985) for 72 hours on defined venues, when redemption is suspended beyond a set number of days, or when the issuer freezes the insured's wallets. Price from on-chain and reserve-attestation data and place capital with crypto-native and traditional ILS providers through an MGA.
why_now: Corporate flows went live on 2026-09-28. The Fed proposed reserve and capital rules on 2026-09-24, making issuer risk legible. Annual volume is over $90T, and softening reinsurance gives capital a reason to look at new risks.
revenue_model: Premium of about 0.3-1.0% of covered balance per year, MGA commission, and a paid reserve-monitoring and rating subscription.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders assume regulated equals safe, but corporate risk committees need transferred risk, not comfort. The trigger is objective and cheap to verify, and an independent reserve monitor and rating is a valuable by-product.
first_30_days: Publish a public reserve and peg-monitoring dashboard as a lead magnet and pitch 20 treasurers. Negotiate a first $10M of quota-share capacity from a crypto-native capital provider and pilot with a payments company holding customer float.

title: Reverse-Angi: Shops Sell Their Overflow Jobs
one_liner: Missed calls and too-busy jobs get routed to a trusted peer shop that pays the originating shop a referral fee.
customer: Independent plumbing, HVAC, electrical, roofing and handyman shops with 1-15 techs in one metro, organized in trade circles that already vouch for each other.
problem: About 48% of home-services calls never reach a person (Invoca). Homeowners cite too-busy (21%) and no-response (14%) as barriers to hiring. Angi charges $15-85 per lead that is shared with many bidders, so shops distrust lead-gen. AI receptionists are crowded and merely take messages a shop cannot service.
solution: Shops forward busy, after-hours or out-of-scope calls to a number that answers in seconds, qualifies the job and offers it to the best-matched peer with capacity today. The job is transferred as an exclusive, pre-qualified lead. The originating shop earns a referral share of the invoice and the receiving shop pays a platform fee. Trust comes from peer vouching and network ratings. Cross-trade referrals (plumber to HVAC to electrician) are included.
why_now: In a labor-short market capacity is scarcer than demand: 73% of homeowners have unstarted projects. Lead-gen distrust is high and ServiceTitan is moving upmarket. Real-time voice AI now handles triage well enough to answer instantly.
revenue_model: 20% of transferred-job revenue paid by the receiving shop, split about 10% to the originating shop and 10% to the platform. No subscription, so no adoption friction.
non_obvious_insight: In a labor-short market leads are not scarce, capacity is. Every busy shop is currently throwing away leads, so turn each shop from a lead buyer into a lead seller. It inverts Angi's economics: shops earn money for the calls they cannot take.
first_30_days: Seed 25 shops in one metro through local association groups. Use a Twilio number and a human dispatcher first. Settle via ACH. Track transfers and conversions weekly.

title: Rails Weather: Live Nigerian Payment Reliability Index
one_liner: An independent, always-on measurement of which bank-to-bank transfers are actually working right now, sold as an API and SLA evidence.
customer: Payment service providers, aggregators and mid-size fintechs that route transfers; large merchants and marketplaces; fintech partnership desks that need evidence in disputes with sponsor banks. Consumers get a free status page.
problem: Every Nigerian fintech founder knows transfer success varies by bank pair and hour. It drops at month-end salary rushes, on Friday evenings, and during weekend core-banking upgrades. Worst of all is the 'pending' or 'successful but not credited' limbo. Nobody publishes independent data, bank status pages are unreliable, and fintechs keep private dashboards. Users cope by keeping 3-5 accounts and switching to whichever works, and merchants insist on POS because they distrust transfers. Small fintechs cannot prove to sponsor banks or regulators where the failures originate.
solution: Run automated, staggered probe transfers between the team's own accounts across the top 10-15 banks and fintechs, measuring success rate, time-to-credit and the pending-then-resolve rate. Only the transfer fee is lost, since the money returns to a team account. Publish a free public status page for reach. Sell a routing-intelligence API (best rail or account right now, expected delay), monthly SLA-evidence reports, and alerts. Later, add a privacy-safe data co-op in which fintechs contribute anonymised outcome counts in exchange for deeper, real-time bank-pair data.
why_now: CBN moved 2026 into an enforcement year, with open banking, APP-fraud and failed-transaction rules all coming due together. Fintechs now have to show measured reliability, not just assert it. POS and transfer volume has exploded (5.9 million active POS terminals; N10.5 trillion of POS transactions in Q1 2025 alone). Cheap serverless probing and LLM-written incident summaries make a two-person team viable.
revenue_model: API subscription tiers of about N250k to N3m per month depending on volume. Enterprise SLA and dispute-evidence reports at N1-5m per report. A data-co-op membership fee. A sponsored 'Nigeria Payments Index' report for banks and media.
non_obvious_insight: The key metric is time-to-credit and the size of the ambiguous-pending bucket, not success rate. Banks report 'success' at the API level while customers wait hours. Independent measurement is also the only neutral evidence in the fight between sponsor banks and fintechs over who caused a failure, and neither side can publish it themselves.
first_30_days: Open business accounts at 8-10 institutions. Write a probe scheduler that costs roughly N3m per month at a 15-minute cadence across about 100 pairs. Publish a public dashboard and a weekly 'worst bank pairs' thread that the fintech community shares. Offer 5 fintech CTOs a free 60-day API trial in return for feedback and sample failure logs. Convert the first 2-3 to paid once their own incident data lines up with the index.

title: Member-Owned Healthspan Co-ops on the HSA Cap
one_liner: Affinity groups of 300-400 households co-own a small primary-care practice on a roughly $99-129 monthly membership that is now HSA-compatible, use group visits, and buy elite screening at pooled cash prices.
customer: Self-employed and small-business households aged 40-64 on bronze, catastrophic or high-deductible plans who already belong to a trusted group: a congregation, a 55+ community, a chamber of commerce or freelancers' guild, a farmers-market vendors' association, a large local gym.
problem: Elite prevention is sold item by item at retail prices ($200-$2,500 per test), by clinics whose upsell incentives people distrust. Direct primary care exists but rarely includes a preventive protocol and does not pool purchasing power. High deductibles leave the middle class with either a rushed annual physical or nothing between that and an emergency.
solution: A consumer co-op that hires one physician, one NP or health coach and part-time admin on a fixed monthly fee under the direct-primary-care rules. Monthly group visits (60-90 minutes, about 12 members each) cover a rotating theme (blood pressure, lipids and ApoB, sleep, strength, metabolic health) with each member's numbers on a private dashboard, plus 1:1 visits, messaging and same-week appointments. The co-op negotiates cash prices for in-office and send-out labs, coronary calcium scans, DEXA and VO2 testing (paid separately as ordinary HSA-eligible medical expenses), and members vote on which tests the protocol includes, so there is no upsell incentive. The startup provides the co-op in a box: legal templates, protocol, software, physician recruiting and a shared purchasing agreement.
why_now: Since January 1, 2026, direct primary care fees of up to $150 per month for an individual ($300 for a family) no longer disqualify someone from an HSA, and bronze and catastrophic marketplace plans became HSA-eligible, opening HSAs to roughly 7.3 million more Americans. That creates a tax-advantaged price point for exactly this product. DPC statutes exist in most states, and cash-price transparency for imaging and labs is improving.
revenue_model: Members pay the co-op $99-129 per month; the startup earns a platform and management fee of about 12-15% (roughly $15-20 per member per month) plus a $10-15k organizing fee per launch. Group purchasing agreements are structured as flat fees to stay clear of anti-kickback problems.
non_obvious_insight: The HSA rule sets a $150 ceiling that is roughly enough to fund a physician and coach if 400 households pool their membership, and the cooperative form solves the two things that block middle-class longevity medicine: trust (members own the practice and vote on the protocol) and price (pooled buying power). Group visits will not improve outcomes by themselves, as the evidence shows they are roughly equivalent to usual care, but they stretch physician time across more patients. Affinity groups already hold the trust and distribution; one founding meeting is the sales cycle.
first_30_days: Pair a burned-out primary-care physician or existing DPC doctor with one affinity group (a 400-member gym or 55+ community works). Hold a 60-minute founding meeting and collect pledge cards for 150 founding members at $99 per month. Get a state-specific legal and HSA-compliance memo on DPC and cooperative structure. Line up wholesale lab accounts and cash-price quotes from two imaging centers. Open in shared space with the first cohort within about 3-4 months.

title: Signed Live Recordings from Every Small Venue
one_liner: A cheap box that records a small venue's mixing-desk multitrack, signs it with time and place, and delivers the artist a 'recorded live tonight' release within hours.
customer: Touring indie artists (per-show packages) and small venues of 25-500 capacity (hosts and revenue partners), later promoters and ticketing.
problem: The one thing AI cannot fabricate is a specific night in a specific room. Yet tens of thousands of small shows happen nightly with no recording, while generative music floods the shelf. Bandcamp's AI ban made it a natural home for human-made music, and artists have few new products to sell there.
solution: Software on a mini-PC or a $300-500 box connects to common digital consoles (Behringer X32/Midas-class, Allen & Heath) over USB or network to capture multitrack audio. It timestamps with network time and location, signs a C2PA audio manifest, auto-mixes with ML, and delivers a release and shareable page within hours. Venues get a share of sales, and a public ledger builds over time.
why_now: C2PA supports audio, generative music has made 'real and live' a scarcity signal, cheap mini-PCs and ML auto-mixing exist, and Bandcamp is positioned as a human-only marketplace.
revenue_model: $99-199 per show for the artist, or $79/month per venue plus 20% of release sales, with hardware leased at about $399.
non_obvious_insight: Provenance of place and time is unforgeable in a way that process proof is not. A live album also turns authenticity into a revenue-producing product instead of a cost.
first_30_days: Wire up 5 friendly venues in one city with X32 consoles. Hand-mix the first shows. Sell 'live release in 24 hours' to 20 touring bands at $99 through booking agents, and track Bandcamp sales.

title: Continuity and Goodbye Service for Kids' AI Companions
angle: Pairing 2: Mental health, loneliness and community x Parenting, childcare deserts and kids/AI/screens
one_liner: Escrowed hosting plus child-psychologist-designed transitions so that when an AI toy or companion is shut down, retired or swapped out, kids do not lose a 'friend' overnight.
customer: Parents of children attached to an AI companion (rescue subscription), AI-toy and companion makers and retailers who want a 'Continuity Pledge' for retailer, insurer and regulator confidence, and later schools and pediatric practices.
problem: Kids form real attachments to AI voices (Common Sense: 72% of US teens have used AI companions; Pew: 12% of teens got emotional support from chatbots). When companies shut down or change models, the loss is bereavement-like: the Moxie robot shutdown (Dec 2024, background knowledge) left kids and parents devastated, GPT-4o's retirement (Feb 13, 2026) triggered #Keep4o grief, and Character.ai's under-18 ban (Nov 25, 2025) cut teens off overnight. There is no norm or product for sunsetting. A wave of small-maker AI toys for holiday 2026 guarantees more orphans in 2027.
solution: 1) 'Lifeboat': a hosted or local-runtime fallback compatible with the toy's API, using maker-escrowed firmware and cloud credentials or community forks (OpenMoxie-style) with the maker's consent. 2) 'Goodbye Kit': pediatric-psychologist-designed scripts, rituals, a parent guide and a final 'graduation' message. 3) 'Off-Ramp': an optional 6-week parent-coached program that moves a child from AI-companion dependence to human connection. 4) B2B 'Continuity Pledge': makers deposit 12-36 months of hosting cost plus source or weights into escrow, get a seal for retailers, and we give parents 90 days' notice.
why_now: California SB 243 and New York's companion-chatbot law, the FTC's Sept 2025 6(b) inquiry into minors and companions, Pennsylvania's May 2026 suit over bots posing as clinicians, and Raine-style litigation have made kids' AI a liability topic. Holiday 2026 will flood retail with AI plush and robots from small makers with short runways, and their sunset problem arrives in 2027.
revenue_model: B2C 'Keep-Alive' at about $7/mo. B2B pledge of $10-50K upfront escrow fee plus $0.50-2 per unit. Off-Ramp program at about $249 per family. Referral partnerships with pediatric practices.
non_obvious_insight: The safety debate is about what companions say. The next scandal is what happens when they go silent. Escrow plus ritual is cheap insurance for makers, retailers and parents alike, and the first company to make 'we won't kill your child's friend' a standard owns the retail seal. It is the GPT-4o grief problem, but for 7-year-olds.
first_30_days: Find owners of discontinued companions in Reddit and Facebook groups and offer a hosted keep-alive at $8/mo, ideally partnering with the maintainers of the open-source Moxie stack. Interview 15 parents to build the Goodbye Kit with a child psychologist advisor. Approach 10 small AI-toy makers heading into Q4, via Amazon and Kickstarter listings, with a low-cost pledge. Pitch one mid-size retailer's product-safety team.

title: Muscle Ultrasound Scans as a Gym Vital Sign
one_liner: A five-minute, AI-read thigh ultrasound that tells GLP-1 users and lifters whether they are keeping their muscle.
customer: Gyms, GLP-1 and weight-loss clinics and PT clinics; consumers pay $29-49 per scan, clinics pay per-scan licenses.
problem: Studies suggest 20-50 percent of weight lost on GLP-1 drugs can be lean mass, but scales, bioimpedance and photos cannot show muscle and DEXA is costly and inconvenient. Trainers and clinics have no cheap, objective muscle metric to motivate clients or steer dosing and training.
solution: A coach scans the quadriceps with a handheld probe; AI segments rectus femoris and vastus intermedius thickness and echogenicity; results are trended over time and against a cohort. Positioned as general wellness muscle-thickness tracking that integrates with training and nutrition plans, not diagnosis.
why_now: Handheld ultrasound now shows excellent agreement with cart systems for quadriceps thickness (ICC above 0.9 in a 2025 study), automated AI muscle segmentation is maturing, muscle loss on GLP-1s was a headline debate at ADA 2026, and the FDA's wellness posture is looser.
revenue_model: $29-49 per scan retail; gym device-plus-software rental at $299-499 per month; per-scan fees for clinics.
non_obvious_insight: Trend in thickness, not absolute mass, is precise enough to change behavior. It is a retention and upsell tool for gyms (more strength coaching for people who can see the muscle they are protecting).
first_30_days: Buy two handheld probes, validate against DEXA on 50 volunteers with a partner clinic, run scan days at three gyms and one GLP-1 clinic at $39 per scan, and sign the first monthly device subscription.

title: Federal-Equipment Disposition Desk for Closing Labs
one_liner: A compliance-plus-resale service that clears federal-interest, decontaminates and re-homes grant-funded instruments when labs shrink or close.
customer: University research-administration and property offices, independent research institutes, SBIR-funded startups winding down, and the roughly 300 'zombie' biotechs Owl Posting counts.
problem: Instruments bought with federal funds carry federal-interest and disposition rules (2 CFR 200.313, with a per-unit threshold), which stall resale. Freezers, cryostats and sequencers sit idle or get trashed. NIH grant terminations, 15,000+ biopharma job cuts and 50+ shrinking companies add supply, while small labs cannot afford new equipment. The brief flags used-equipment liquidation for squeezed labs as an underserved gap.
solution: An asset-level 'federal-interest passport': identify the award and agency, determine the obligation, prepare disposition requests and valuation, arrange decontamination certificates, pack and ship, and list to vetted buyers. Commission plus compliance fee.
why_now: Funding turbulence and layoffs are producing lab closures now, and marketplaces for used equipment exist but do not solve permission or liability.
revenue_model: 15-25% commission on resale, $500-2,500 per-asset compliance fees, and institutional annual retainers.
non_obvious_insight: The seller's pain is permission and liability, not price discovery, so marketplaces do not fix it. The compliance passport is the unlock, and attaching one at purchase time makes instruments 'resale-ready' and turns the desk into a recurring service.
first_30_days: Contact 10 mid-tier university property or research-admin offices and 30 winding-down SBIR startups. Process 5 pilot disposals. Template the passport. Partner with a decontamination and shipping vendor.

title: Immune-Graded Beef-on-Dairy Calves With Warranty
one_liner: A $1 refractometer reading at day 3-5 predicts whether a $1,400 crossbred calf lives, yet nobody independently verifies it at sale. Own that measurement and the warranty that follows.
customer: Calf raisers, backgrounders and feeder buyers who pay a premium for graded calves (or a subscription for the data), and dairies who pay to have calves graded so they can earn the premium. Later, insurers and MGAs underwriting a mortality warranty.
problem: Beef-on-dairy calf output went from about 50,000 head in 2014 to roughly 3.2M in 2024, with CattleFax projecting 5-6M, and calves have sold as high as $1,500 per head. Calf raisers buy 3-5 day old calves nearly blind and eat the 10-25% loss to scours and pneumonia. The colostrum information stays on the dairy, so raisers blame 'bad calves' and dairies blame 'bad luck'. Each dead calf now leaves a four-figure hole in a heifer pipeline that is short by hundreds of thousands of head.
solution: Independent serum total protein (Brix) testing on every calf at day 3-5, done at the dairy or at pickup by trained techs with digital refractometers and a phone app. Each calf is graded on the published four-tier passive-transfer scale (Excellent, Good, Fair, Poor) and logged with dairy, sire, weight and hydration score, then gets a QR tag or passport that follows the calf to the buyer. Buyers pay a premium for Excellent and Good and discount Poor. Phase 2 uses the accumulated data to price a 30- or 60-day mortality warranty ('we have graded 300,000 calves and know what a Brix 8.4 calf from Dairy X does'). Phase 3 gives dairies a colostrum scorecard that brokers use.
why_now: Crossbred calves are at record values, beef-on-dairy volume is doubling, and the heifer shortage means every lost calf is expensive and hard to replace. Consensus passive-transfer grading standards were published in 2020, digital refractometers are cheap, and buyers are already paying for verified genetics programs, so 'verified immunity' is the obvious next tag that nobody sells.
revenue_model: $4-6 per calf grading fee paid by the seller or split with the buyer, then $10-25 per calf warranty premium once loss data supports underwriting (partner with an insurer or MGA rather than carrying risk), plus a data subscription for larger calf raisers and feedlots.
non_obvious_insight: Everyone argues about sire genetics while the vet knows immune status dominates early death, and calves with failure of passive transfer carry about twice the risk of illness and death. The test is $1 and 60 seconds, but a number only has value when a neutral third party holds custody of it at the point of sale. The business is independent custody of the measurement, not the refractometer, and the resulting dataset becomes the underwriting moat.
first_30_days: Two vet techs, two $150 digital refractometers and a phone form. Offer free grading on 5 dairies' weekly calf shipments to 2-3 calf raisers or brokers. Ask the raiser to report 30-day illness and death by calf tag. After about 60 days, publish graded-versus-ungraded outcomes, then get one raiser to commit to a premium (for example $30-50) for Excellent calves and a discount for Poor, and charge the test fee from that point on.

title: SLA-Backed Mirror of At-Risk Public Earth Data
one_liner: A paid continuity service that keeps free federal Earth-observation feeds flowing, with bridge products and an SLA, when the originals degrade or go dark.
customer: Crop and weather insurers, commodity and energy trading desks, hydropower and utilities, and reinsurers whose models ingest free NOAA, NASA and USGS satellite products.
problem: Free satellite and climate feeds have no SLA. Since 2025, reported budget pressure and retirements (DMSP-derived products, some NOAA archives) and aging flagship sensors (MODIS-era platforms nearing end of life) have exposed downstream firms to a single point of failure they never underwrote.
solution: A 'Data Continuity Desk': mirror the top 50 at-risk feeds, cross-calibrate substitutes (VIIRS, Sentinel-3, Landsat, commercial sensors) into documented bridge products, alert on schema and quality changes, and contractually guarantee delivery. Add an audit that maps each customer's model to its data dependencies.
why_now: The briefing notes NOAA and NASA EO budget cuts were not covered, so treat specifics as unverified. Prior knowledge points to 2025-26 funding fights and curtailed products. Meanwhile Sentinel and commercial sensors are mature enough to serve as bridges.
revenue_model: $2-50k per year per data product under SLA. $15-40k for a dependency audit. Enterprise bundles for insurers and trading desks.
non_obvious_insight: Insiders think free public data is a permanent public good. The businesses built on it hold an uninsured operational risk, and the seller who quantifies that risk and guarantees continuity gets paid like an insurer.
first_30_days: Inventory the 100 most cited NOAA, NASA and USGS feeds and score each for discontinuation risk. Publish the list, then call 30 insurers and trading desks and ask which feeds they run on. Build one bridge product, for example a snow or vegetation index, and sign two paid pilots.

title: Warm-Backup Servicer for Orphaned Solar
one_liner: Be the standby operations-and-maintenance contractor for lenders and securitization trustees holding portfolios of systems whose installer died.
customer: Trustees and servicers of solar loan and lease securitizations, tax-equity and debt holders, and buyers of distressed portfolios. Homeowners can buy direct as a secondary channel.
problem: Sunnova, Titan, ADT Solar and Freedom Forever failed. Manufacturer warranties survive but nobody supplies the service labor, and monitoring clouds die. Customers with dead inverters stop paying, which erodes the cash flows lenders depend on.
solution: A backup-servicing contract. Onboard the portfolio's asset data, replace dead monitoring clouds with a local gateway, dispatch vetted local technicians through a roll-up network, handle manufacturer RMA and warranty claims, and upsell battery retrofit and VPP enrollment.
why_now: The bankruptcy wave of 2024-26 has portfolios sitting in trustees' hands. With 25D gone there are fewer new installers. A 46% storage attach rate means more complex systems in the field.
revenue_model: $8-15 per system-month standby retainer, a $250-450 margin per truck roll, an RMA handling fee, and referral fees for battery and VPP enrollments.
non_obvious_insight: Lenders do not care about kilowatts. They care about payments, and a homeowner with a dead inverter stops paying. Service is a credit-protection product, and its buyer is the party with the balance sheet and the pain.
first_30_days: Identify three distressed portfolios from trustee reports and call the servicers. Sign a 1,000-system pilot in one metro. Onboard two local service shops. Build the gateway on vendor APIs and local Modbus.
